alt: Six cause-and-effect chains. Meat needs more land, water and feed per calorie; climate change lowers staple yields unevenly; biofuels compete with food; the 2022 invasion of Ukraine disrupted Black Sea exports and raised world prices; antibiotic overuse drives resistance; longer lives raise chronic disease and care costs.
caption: Each pressure works through a different chain, but all squeeze food or health systems.

alt: A food supply chain from farm to consumer. Food loss happens between harvest and retail through poor storage and pests; food waste happens at retail and consumer level. In lower-income countries most is lost after harvest, needing storage and cold chains; in higher-income countries more is wasted, needing labelling, redistribution and behaviour change.
caption: Where food goes missing in the chain decides the right response.

alt: Three technology options with a benefit and a catch each. Precision agriculture cuts waste of inputs but is costly for small farmers. Drought- or flood-tolerant varieties improve resilience but must reach farmers at affordable prices. Vertical farming uses little land and water but has high energy costs and suits high-value crops rather than staples.
caption: Every technology fix has a catch, often about cost and who can use it.

after: ### Case study: Ethiopia's Productive Safety Net Programme
alt: Flow of the programme: chronically food-insecure rural households work on community projects such as soil and water conservation, terracing and roads, and receive food or cash. Predictable support replaces emergency appeals and protects assets in drought, building resilience. Limits: it depends on donor funding and cannot overcome conflict or extreme drought alone.
caption: Predictable food or cash for work builds resilience, but relies on donors.
